beliefs.limiting: I’ve smoked too long. It’s too late.
beliefs.counterpart: Most people hooked on nicotine get free in the end. Plenty of the ex-smokers I know smoked longer than I have.
beliefs.test: This week, ask two or three ex-smokers you know how long they smoked before they stopped for good. Notice how many had smoked as long as you, or longer.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 1,300 of 6,937 people ever hooked on nicotine were already free when asked. A projected 83.7% get free in their lifetime, likely on the high side.

refs.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction 106(3):657-69.
refs.quote: Life-time cumulative probability estimates of dependence remission were 83.7% for nicotine … Nicotine remission (N=1,300)
refs.note: NESARC 2001–2002, face-to-face interviews with 43,093 US adults; 6,937 had lifetime DSM-IV nicotine dependence. 1,300 is the unweighted count in the Table 3/4 header (18.7%). 'Free' means they had finally stopped having any sign of dependence, with none coming back, as they recalled it. The authors warn that self-report overstates remission.

problems: Rule 10 broken: the proof opens with the hopeful projection. The full text has a counted figure. The rest holds. NESARC 2001–2002 ran face-to-face interviews with 43,093 US adults; 6,937 had lifetime DSM-IV nicotine dependence. 83.7% is a lifetime cumulative estimate made by the actuarial method, and the paper calls it a projection. 'Lose every sign of it' fits the paper's definition ('finally stopped having any of these experiences … never started happening again'). Severity 'dependent' fits.
'Likely on the high side' is supported. The limitations say self-report leads to 'overreport of remission' and that the age of remission is open to recall bias.

beliefs.limiting: Quitting will be hell. I can’t handle the withdrawal.
beliefs.counterpart: I’ve got through rougher weeks than this. And this one ends.
beliefs.test: Pick one ordinary day this week. Push your first cigarette, vape or pouch back two hours. Every 15 minutes, rate the urge 0–10 on paper. Notice whether it stays at the top or rises and falls.
beliefs.proof: A review of 120 studies: withdrawal peaks in week 1 and lasts 2–4 weeks. In 214 smokers who quit in a clinic group, each symptom tracked was back to pre-quit level within 10 days. Neither includes craving.

refs.cite: Shiffman S, Patten C, Gwaltney C, Paty J, Gnys M, Kassel J, Hickcox M, Waters A, Balabanis M (2006). Natural history of nicotine withdrawal. Addiction 101(12):1822-32.
refs.quote: All symptoms returned to baseline levels within 10 days of quitting.
refs.note: 214 cigarette smokers in a clinic-based behavioural group cessation programme who quit for at least 24 hours; electronic diary for up to 21 days. Symptoms tracked: negative affect, arousal, attention, restlessness, sleep, cognitive performance; craving is not listed. Group averages, so some people take longer.

refs.cite: Hughes JR (2007). Effects of abstinence from tobacco: valid symptoms and time course. Nicotine & Tobacco Research 9(3):315-27.
refs.quote: Anger, anxiety, depression, difficulty concentrating, impatience, insomnia, and restlessness are valid withdrawal symptoms that peak within the first week and last 2-4 weeks.
refs.note: One author's review of 120 studies (1990–2004) of smokers who stopped, read on his own judgement. Craving, hunger and performance were left out of the review.

beliefs.origin: new (the withdrawal proof comes from 06-template.json nicotine belief 2)

problems: 'Every withdrawal symptom was back to its pre-quit level within 10 days' reads more hopeful than the source. Shiffman's 'All symptoms' means only the ones it tracked: negative affect, arousal, attention, restlessness, sleep and cognitive performance. Craving is not among them, and Hughes says outright that his review leaves craving out. The plan's step 2 proof says cue craving is stronger at day 35, so the reader gets two claims that seem to clash.
Rule 10 (cautious first): the 10-day figure is the hopeful one. Hughes's 'peak within the first week and last 2-4 weeks' is the cautious one and should come first.
Hughes 2007 is one author's review of 120 studies, and the abstract says 'Data collection and interpretation were based solely on the author's subjective judgments.' That belongs in the note.

Shiffman: 214 smokers in a clinic-based behavioural group programme who quit for at least 24 hours, tracked with an electronic diary for up to 21 days. Only the abstract could be fetched; the full text is behind a paywall, and the abstract does not say how many were still off at day 10. Severity 'treatment' fits Shiffman. Hughes mixes populations.
Both quotes are word for word: 11 and 23 words.

beliefs.limiting: A cigarette is the only thing that calms me down.
beliefs.counterpart: When I go a few hours without it, I get edgy. Part of the calm is just that edge going away.
beliefs.test: Next time you go a few hours without it (a flight, a long meeting), rate your stress 0–10 at the start, just before the first one after, and 10 minutes after it. Notice whether it takes you below where you started, or only back to it.
beliefs.proof: In 469 heart patients who wanted to stop, those still off a year later had a bigger drop in stress than those who kept smoking. In 4 studies of anxiety and 3 of stress, both fell more in quitters.

refs.cite: Hajek P, Taylor T, McRobbie H (2010). The effect of stopping smoking on perceived stress levels. Addiction 105(8):1466-71.
refs.quote: abstainers recorded a significantly larger decrease in perceived stress than continuing smokers
refs.note: 469 smokers in hospital after a heart attack or bypass surgery who wanted to stop; 194 stayed off for a year. The authors call them highly dependent smokers.

refs.cite: Taylor G, McNeill A, Girling A, Farley A, Lindson-Hawley N, Aveyard P (2014). Change in mental health after smoking cessation: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 348:g1151.
refs.quote: Four studies reported change in anxiety … Three studies reported change in stress from baseline to follow-up
refs.note: 26 studies in all (11 cohorts, 14 drawn from cessation trials, 1 randomised trial). Anxiety was pooled from 4 studies (7 weeks to 12 months), stress from 3 (6 months to 6 years). Observational, so it shows a link, not proof of cause.

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json nicotine belief 1 (limiting kept word for word; counterpart rewritten from a slogan into something he has felt himself)

problems: 'Across 26 studies' gives the whole review's count, not the studies behind the figure. In the results, 'Four studies reported change in anxiety' and 'Three studies reported change in stress'; the other studies measured depression, quality of life and positive mood. 'Quitters grew less anxious and stressed than smokers' could also be read as a comparison of levels. The source measured change: anxiety and stress fell more in quitters than in people who kept smoking.

Hajek holds. 469 smokers hospitalised after a heart attack or bypass surgery wanted to stop and completed the 1-year follow-up; 194 (41%) stayed off, checked by saliva cotinine. The abstainers had a larger drop in perceived stress. The authors call them 'highly dependent smokers'. The quote is word for word.

Taylor: the conclusion quote is word for word but does not support the counts. The fix gives a quote that does. The review is observational (11 cohorts, 14 secondary analyses of cessation trials, 1 randomised trial), so it shows a link, not proof of cause, as the note says.
Severity 'treatment' fits Hajek (inpatients who wanted to stop). Taylor's populations are mixed.

beliefs.limiting: Just one won’t hurt. I’m still quit.
beliefs.counterpart: Every time I went back, it started with just one.
beliefs.test: Write down the last two or three times you went back after stopping. For each: what the first one was, and how many days until you were back to your usual amount. Notice how often “just one” stayed one.
beliefs.proof: In two small trials, of patch users who smoked at all in week 2, 83% and 97% smoked at 6 months. Of 63 quitters, those assigned two cigarettes after 2 days off relapsed sooner (66 vs 53 in 100).

refs.cite: Kenford SL, Fiore MC, Jorenby DE, Smith SS, Wetter D, Baker TB (1994). Predicting smoking cessation: who will quit with and without the nicotine patch. JAMA 271(8):589-94.
refs.quote: Among active nicotine patch patients who smoked at all during week 2 after quitting, 83% and 97% (studies 1 and 2, respectively) were smoking at 6-month follow-up.
refs.note: Two patch trials of daily smokers (15 or more a day) motivated to quit: 88 and 112 people, about half on a real patch. The abstract does not give how many smoked in week 2, so the groups behind 83% and 97% are smaller.

refs.cite: Shadel WG, Martino SC, Setodji C, Cervone D, Witkiewitz K, Beckjord EB, Scharf D, Shih R (2011). Lapse-induced surges in craving influence relapse in adult smokers: an experimental investigation. Health Psychology 30(5):588-96.
refs.quote: Whereas 53.1% of participants in the no lapse condition relapsed, 65.5% of participants in the lapse condition did so.
refs.note: 63 adults (15 or more a day) who quit with a brief behavioural programme, randomly told after 48 hours off to smoke two cigarettes (31) or to wait (32); followed 14 days. Relapse = 7 days in a row of smoking. Relapse came sooner after the two cigarettes (HR 2.12, 95% CI 1.03 to 4.35).

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json nicotine belief 5 (limiting kept word for word; counterpart rewritten into his own experience). Both studies are early in a quit; no fetched study measures one cigarette after months off.

problems: Shadel: 'about twice the rate' will be read as twice as many relapsing, and that is wrong. HR 2.12 (95% CI 1.03 to 4.35) is about speed. The full text gives the shares: 'Whereas 53.1% of participants in the no lapse condition relapsed, 65.5% of participants in the lapse condition did so.' Per 100 that is 66 vs 53. The proof also gives no n, and the trial is small: 63 people, 31 told to smoke and 32 told to wait.

Kenford: the 83% and 97% figures and the quote are word for word. The abstract does not give how many active-patch users smoked in week 2, so the groups behind the figures are unknown and smaller than the active-patch halves of 88 and 112. The proof should say the trials are small. The full text is behind a paywall and was not fetched.

Rule 4 holds: both studies count people in treatment (Kenford: patch trials, 15 or more a day, motivated to quit; Shadel: brief CBT programme, 15 or more a day), not ordinary users. Severity 'treatment' fits. 83% comes before 97%, so the cautious figure is first.
Both studies look at slips early in a quit (week 2; after 48 hours off). The origin field already says so.

beliefs.limiting: Vapes and pouches are basically harmless.
beliefs.counterpart: Less harmful, maybe. But I still reach for it all day and get edgy without it.
beliefs.test: For two days, keep a tally of every vape session or pouch on paper, without changing anything. Notice the total, and how many times you reached for it before you had decided to.
beliefs.proof: In 3,609 ex-smokers who vape, dependence was lower than they recalled on cigarettes, but higher with stronger liquid and longer use. A maker-funded test: 6 and 8 mg pouches delivered nicotine as fast and fully as snus and snuff.

refs.cite: Foulds J, Veldheer S, Yingst J, Hrabovsky S, Wilson SJ, Nichols TT, Eissenberg T (2015). Development of a questionnaire for assessing dependence on electronic cigarettes among a large sample of ex-smoking e-cigarette users. Nicotine & Tobacco Research 17(2):186-92.
refs.quote: E-cig dependence appears to vary by product characteristics and liquid nicotine concentration, and it may increase over time.
refs.note: Online survey from December 2012 of 3,609 ex-smokers who now only vape; volunteers from vaping websites, likely pro-vaping (the authors say so). Cigarette dependence was rated from memory (14.5 vs 8.1 on the same 0-20 scale); the liquid-strength analysis used 3,446.

refs.cite: Lunell E, Fagerström K, Hughes J, Pendrill R (2020). Pharmacokinetic comparison of a novel non-tobacco-based nicotine pouch (ZYN) with conventional, tobacco-based Swedish snus and American moist snuff. Nicotine & Tobacco Research 22(10):1757-63.
refs.quote: The two higher doses of ZYN (6 and 8 mg) deliver nicotine as quickly and to a similar extent as existing smokeless products
refs.note: Single-dose randomised crossover study of one brand (ZYN), funded by its maker Swedish Match; one author works there. The abstract does not say who took part or how many.

do: Don’t quit yet. For the next few days, use it the way you always do.
Write down what you think nicotine gives you: calm, focus, a break.
Each time, write one line: the time, where you are, what you wanted from it.
Allow it. No guilt, no promises. You’re studying it, not fighting it.
Ten minutes after each one, ask: did it give me that, or did it just stop the itch?
Most of it is relief from the itch nicotine itself made. Test each one in the table above.
Take each line from step 1 and find something that gives you about 80% of it.
Breaks: step outside anyway, without it. Walk, drink water.
Coffee: change the place or the time for the first weeks.
Hands and mouth: gum, a toothpick, seeds.
Vape or pouch at the desk: put mints, sugar-free gum or a cold drink in the same spot.
Stress: ten slow breaths or a two-minute walk before you decide anything.

proof.text: A lab test, not everyday craving: in groups of about 20 smokers paid to stay off, smoking cues pulled harder at day 35 than at day 7 on some scales. Keep the coffee and break swaps past the first month.

ref.cite: Bedi G, Preston KL, Epstein DH, Heishman SJ, Marrone GF, Shaham Y, de Wit H (2011). Incubation of cue-induced cigarette craving during abstinence in human smokers. Biological Psychiatry 69(7):708-11.
ref.quote: Cue-induced craving was greater in Group 3 (35-day) compared with Group 1 (7-day).
ref.note: 86 non-treatment-seeking smokers of 10 or more a day completed, paid to stay off for 7, 14 or 35 days. The day 35 vs day 7 contrast is between two of three randomised groups that total 62 (from the reported F(1,59)). A lab cue test, not everyday craving.

problems: 'In 86 smokers' is the whole study. The day 35 vs day 7 contrast is between two of three randomised single-session groups (Groups 1–3). The reported F(1,59) and t(59) mean those three groups total 62, about 20 each. Group 4, which saw cues repeatedly, is not in this contrast. The exact group sizes are in a supplement that was not fetched.

'Pulled harder' holds only 'on some measures', as the abstract says. Groups 3 and 1 differed on the TCQ-SF craving scale, but the groups did not differ on QSU-B Factor 1. The source also says cue-induced craving 'did not decrease with abstinence on any measure'.

The group: non-treatment-seeking smokers of 10 or more a day, paid $30 a day, at the University of Chicago and NIDA in Baltimore. They are heavy users, not checked for dependence, and the plan proof has no severity tag to show this. The proof rightly says 'A lab test, not everyday craving' (rule 19).
The quote is word for word against the PubMed abstract ('compared with'); the PMC manuscript reads 'compared to'.

do: Pick a date a few days to a few weeks out. Write it down and tell one person.
Throw out every pack, vape and pouch the night before.
For three months, nicotine is the one thing. Leave the gym, the diet and the rest of your life as they are.
Treat week 2 as the test: not one puff.
Mark every day you keep. Each one is a complete success, however loud the urge was.
Slipped? Don’t just start again tomorrow. Go back through steps 1–3: what it gave you, which swap was missing, a new date.

proof.text: Without help, most relapses came in the first 8 days of a quit (eight relapse curves from two studies and five untreated groups).

ref.cite: Hughes JR, Keely J, Naud S (2004). Shape of the relapse curve and long-term abstinence among untreated smokers. Addiction 99(1):29-38.
ref.quote: The existing eight relapse curves from two studies of self-quitters and five no-treatment control groups indicate most relapse occurs in the first 8 days.

problems: Holds. 'The existing eight relapse curves from two studies of self-quitters and five no-treatment control groups indicate most relapse occurs in the first 8 days.' The quote is word for word, 24 words. 'Without help' fits self-quitters and no-treatment control groups.

Minor, no change needed. The abstract gives no count of people. The review notes the curves were 'heterogeneous' and that there is 'a paucity of studies'. The people were self-quitters, not checked for dependence. The proof is 23 words and claims no more than the source.

do: Say “I don’t smoke”, not “I’m trying to quit”.
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving”, not “I need one”.
When the urge comes with coffee or a drink, it’s the habit asking, not your body.
Offered one? Answer like a non-smoker: “No thanks, I don’t.” No story, no excuse.
At the old moments (after food, on a break), do what a non-smoker does there: nothing.

proof.text: Of 544 ex-smokers in Australia and the UK, 14 still called themselves smokers trying to quit. A year later 10 of those 14 smoked again, against 7 to 8 in 100 who called themselves ex-smokers or non-smokers.

ref.cite: Callaghan L, Yong HH, Borland R, Cummings KM, Hitchman SC, Fong GT (2021). What kind of smoking identity following quitting would elevate smokers relapse risk? Addictive Behaviors 112:106654.
ref.quote: Participants who described themselves as ‘A smoker trying to quit’ at baseline (Wave 9) had the highest rates of relapse (71.4%) at follow-up survey (Wave 10)
ref.note: 544 former smokers, quit a month or more, in the ITC surveys in Australia and the UK, 2013-14; relapse self-reported at 12 months. Groups: 14 'smoker trying to quit' (71.4% relapsed), 150 ex-smokers (7.2%), 251 non-smokers (8%), 129 'smoker who has chosen to no longer smoke' (12.4%). The authors call the first group small. A link, not proof of cause.

problems: The n behind the comparison is not 544. Table 2 shows only 14 people still called themselves 'a smoker trying to quit', and 71.4% of them (10 of 14) relapsed. The comparison groups were 150 ex-smokers (7.2% relapsed) and 251 non-smokers (8%). The authors say 'the number of participants who identified as a smoker trying to quit was small'. Rule 17 says the proof must name this weakness, and per-100 figures make the gap readable.

The rest holds. The sample is 544 former smokers (quit a month or more) from ITC Australia (304) and UK (240), Waves 9 (2013) and 10 (2014), a non-treatment-seeking cohort, with relapse self-reported at the 12-month follow-up. The original quote is word for word. The link is observational, so the note's 'a link, not proof of cause' stays.

do: Help is a tool, not a must. Use it to make the date stick, not to put it off.
Ask a doctor about varenicline.
Or use a patch plus gum or lozenge, not just one.
Still on cigarettes? A vape helps more smokers stop than patches do. It’s a switch, not an exit.
Quitting a vape? Ask about varenicline too: in two small trials it helped vapers stop.
Put money on it: give a friend a sum to hand back at month 3.

proof.text: In 41 trials (17,395 people), 23 in 100 on varenicline were still off cigarettes at 6 months or more, against 10 in 100 on a dummy pill.

ref.cite: Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, Theodoulou A, Hajizadeh A, Hartman L, Lindson N (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 5:CD006103.
ref.quote: For every 100 people using varenicline to stop smoking, 21 to 25 might successfully stop
ref.note: Summary of findings table 1, abstinence at longest follow-up (6+ months), varenicline vs placebo: 99 per 1000 with placebo, 230 per 1000 (213 to 249) with varenicline; RR 2.32; 41 studies, 17,395 people; high certainty.

problems: Rule 12a: 'about 2.3 times as many' is a relative risk. The rule says a what-helps figure gives per 100 with and per 100 without, never '×'. The review's Summary of findings table gives 99 per 1000 with placebo and 230 per 1000 (213 to 249) with varenicline for abstinence at 6+ months: 23 in 100 vs 10 in 100. Leaving out the absolute rates makes the figure look more hopeful, because it hides that most people on varenicline did not stay off.

The rest holds. RR 2.32 (2.15 to 2.51), 41 studies, 17,395 participants, high certainty. The quote is word for word, 27 words. The people were smokers in cessation trials, so severity 'treatment' fits.

Outside the proof, not checked against a source, no field changed: the step 5 actions 'A vape helps more smokers stop than patches do' and 'in two small trials it helped vapers stop' carry no proof of their own.
